title: The center of the Milky Way
caption: The center of the Milky Way in infrared light, imaged by the Very Large Telescope
celestial: Milky Way Galactic Center · constellation Sagittarius

recognition.text: Official ESO press-release image. No published audience rating.

story: Thousands of individual stars crowd this infrared view of the center of our Milky Way, in the southern constellation Sagittarius, the Archer. Their colors tell their temperatures, with blue stars hot and red stars cool, and between them glows infrared light from dust.

The galactic center is "only" 26,000 light-years away, close enough that sharp images can pick out stars within the central region, just one light-year wide. By tracking how those stars move, astronomers can measure the gravity that steers them.

Over about a decade, those measurements showed that roughly 3 million times the mass of the Sun is packed within just 10 light-days of a compact radio and X-ray source called Sagittarius A*. That makes it the most likely match for the black hole believed to sit at the heart of our galaxy.

understand.summary: This image was taken with the NACO instrument on ESO's Very Large Telescope, combining three infrared wavebands. The stars' colors indicate temperature, blue for hot and red for cool.
filters: 2.18 μm · Infrared K (Very Large Telescope NACO)
understand.eye: Infrared light is invisible to the eye, and in visible light thick dust hides this region from view.

behind.exposure: Not published on the source page.
behind.technique: Not stated by the source (single frame, stack, mosaic or panorama unknown).

explore: The picture was made with the NACO instrument on the 8.2-meter VLT Yepun telescope, combining frames taken in three infrared bands spanning 1.6 to 3.5 micrometers. A newer image of the same region was published in 2008.
alt: A dense field of thousands of stars in blue and red, with a diffuse glow of dust between them.
